cim: AI as a New Tribe: Professor Alan Macfarlane on what makes us human

szoveg_eredeti:
What might an anthropologist make of artificial intelligence if he approached it as an unfamiliar tribe?

What might an anthropologist make of artificial intelligence if he approached it as an unfamiliar tribe?

That question framed an SCMP Plus fireside chat with Professor Alan Macfarlane at The Center in Central, Hong Kong, on October 26. Speaking with SCMP senior AI technology reporter Vincent Chow, Macfarlane explored how AI changes knowledge creation and sharing, and what distinguishes its capabilities from human experience.

An emeritus professor of anthropological science at the University of Cambridge and Life Fellow of King’s College, Macfarlane looked at AI through the lens of human history and culture, considering its implications for education, work and future generations.

.css-1mniedq{color:inherit;font-weight:inherit;font-size:inherit;font-family:inherit;line-height:inherit;}Understanding AI as a new tribe

Macfarlane invited the audience to consider AI as an unfamiliar culture: exploring its origins, how it operates and its place within society.

He situated AI within successive revolutions in communication, from speech and writing to printing and computing. Each transformed how people created, preserved and transmitted knowledge; AI, he argued, represents another major shift.

Despite its digital nature, AI depends on resource-intensive physical infrastructure, Macfarlane emphasised, including data centres, electricity supplies and semiconductor manufacturing.

Macfarlane distinguished between processing information and experiencing the world.

Drawing on his experiments with ChatGPT, he questioned whether discussing death, beauty or pain amounted to understanding those experiences. In his view, AI’s apparent intelligence derives from sophisticated pattern recognition and the human knowledge used in its training, rather than conscious experience.

He encouraged curiosity rather than fear, while acknowledging the limits of AI’s capabilities and our own understanding.

Different perspectives, shared challenges

The conversation also explored contrasting attitudes towards AI in China and the United States.

Chow noted how much of the US debate focused on consciousness and new forms of intelligence, but in China the emphasis was often on practical applications and everyday problem-solving.

Macfarlane suggested that cultural and philosophical traditions help shape these perspectives, influencing how societies understand technology and imagine its role in human progress.

During the audience Q&A, discussion turned to education, employment and digital technology’s impact on younger generations.

Macfarlane emphasised the importance of helping children understand both AI’s opportunities and risks, while preserving time for creativity and human interaction.

Looking ahead, he offered a cautiously optimistic view: if managed thoughtfully, automation could relieve people of repetitive labour, creating more time for civic life, leisure and creative pursuits.
